I think it is one of the best puzzle games I have ever played, and I would highly recommend it. The game drops you into a mysterious magic performance filled with hidden secrets, where you sit in the audience and watch Mr. Rabbit perform on a small stage. While the show unfolds, you will constantly interact with the stage as you play, clicking on the magic hat, opening curtains, and exploring different props. Every small action can trigger something unexpected, which makes it feel like the performance is alive and reacting to you. What I really like is how the game keeps making me question what is real and what is just part of the trick. Each act feels like a short puzzle, but there are almost no direct instructions, so you are always observing carefully and trying things out on your own. The atmosphere is also very unique. It starts off cozy and playful, almost like a charming little magic show, but slowly it begins to build layers of mystery and a subtle sense of unease.

The Mr. Rabbit Magic Show is a free 10-year anniversary tribute game to the Rusty Lake franchise. Most of the game is spent completing various point and click puzzles to get through the various “acts” of Mr. Rabbit’s onstage “magic show”. The finale becomes a bit meta with you completing tasks for the game devs of Rusty Lake in their studio. It’s fairly standard while lacking most of the intrigue, atmosphere, and magic from previous titles, even some of the shorter ones. Despite being a bit more stripped back, there is a very good jazz track that plays for most of the game and other atmospheric ambience that make it solid enough. I will say it still contains a few tricks up its sleeve and clever puzzles to keep you entertained while you wait for their next title, “Servant of the Lake”. The game is free and it’s an entertaining enough walk back through the past, so I recommend this for fans of the Rusty Lake franchise.

The Mr. Rabbit Magic Show developed and published by Rusty Lake is a short but delightfully inventive puzzle experience that serves as both a playful celebration of the studio’s distinctive style and a clever theatrical showcase for its signature surreal storytelling. Designed as an interactive magic performance, the game invites players to step into the audience of an unusual stage show hosted by the enigmatic Mr. Rabbit, a character longtime fans of Rusty Lake will instantly recognize from earlier titles. Rather than presenting a traditional narrative adventure with exploration across multiple locations, the game focuses on a tightly structured series of magical “acts,” each built around a small puzzle that captures the feeling of witnessing a trick unfold in real time.

The structure of the game revolves around a sequence of bite-sized challenges presented as stage illusions. Each act places a set of props on the stage—top hats, playing cards, cages, mirrors, or other mysterious devices—and asks the player to interact with them in order to help Mr. Rabbit complete his trick. The mechanics are simple on the surface, relying mostly on point-and-click interactions, but the puzzles frequently require a bit of lateral thinking. Rusty Lake’s design philosophy has always leaned toward experimentation rather than strict logical deduction, and that approach is very much present here. Solutions often emerge from observing subtle visual hints, manipulating objects in unusual ways, or understanding the playful logic behind a magician’s performance. Some tricks feel like classic puzzle-box challenges, while others rely on visual illusions that cleverly mimic real magic tricks.

Although the game is relatively short, its presentation carries the unmistakable style that defines Rusty Lake’s catalog. The visuals combine minimalistic illustrations with a slightly eerie tone, blending whimsy and unease in equal measure. The stage itself feels like a surreal theater where the boundaries between performance and reality blur. Characters and props are rendered in a clean, hand-drawn style, but their movements and transformations often take on strange or unsettling qualities. Mr. Rabbit himself acts as a charismatic host, silently guiding the player through each act with theatrical gestures and exaggerated expressions. The overall aesthetic reinforces the sensation that something mysterious is always happening just behind the curtain.

Sound design and music contribute significantly to the atmosphere. The soundtrack is playful yet slightly uncanny, echoing the mood of an old magic show mixed with the dreamlike tone Rusty Lake is known for. Subtle sound effects accompany every successful trick or interaction, giving each puzzle the satisfying payoff of a completed illusion. Even though the game does not rely heavily on dialogue or exposition, the audiovisual presentation gives each act a sense of personality and rhythm, making the experience feel like a continuous performance rather than a collection of disconnected puzzles.

While the focus is clearly on puzzle interactions, the game also carries a layer of narrative significance for fans of Rusty Lake’s broader universe. Mr. Rabbit is not simply a random stage performer but a character tied to the surreal mythology that appears throughout the studio’s other games, including titles in the Cube Escape and Rusty Lake series. The magic show occasionally hints at this larger world through subtle references and symbolic imagery. These small touches create a sense that the show is more than just entertainment—it is part of the strange and mysterious timeline that Rusty Lake fans have been piecing together for years.

One of the most memorable elements of the experience arrives when the game begins to break the illusion of the stage itself. What initially appears to be a straightforward sequence of tricks gradually evolves into something more self-aware and experimental. Without revealing too much, the game eventually introduces a playful meta twist that shifts the perspective from a simple stage show into something that feels like a celebration of Rusty Lake’s creative journey. This moment transforms the game from a collection of puzzles into a charming tribute to the studio’s history and its relationship with its audience.

The main drawback of the game lies in its length. Most players will likely complete the entire magic show in less than an hour, and some puzzles may feel too simple for experienced Rusty Lake fans. A few acts end just as they begin to feel interesting, leaving players wishing there were more elaborate sequences or additional layers of challenge. However, the game’s brevity is somewhat intentional. It is designed as a compact, celebratory experience rather than a full-scale adventure, and its pacing reflects the quick, surprising nature of stage magic itself.

Despite its short runtime, the game succeeds in delivering a memorable and creative experience. It captures the playful imagination, surreal charm, and clever puzzle design that have defined Rusty Lake’s identity for years. For longtime followers of the studio, it feels like a lighthearted gift packed with references and personality. For newcomers, it serves as a welcoming introduction to Rusty Lake’s unique blend of mystery and puzzle storytelling.

In the end, The Mr. Rabbit Magic Show may be small in scope, but it demonstrates how much creativity can be packed into a brief interactive performance. Its imaginative presentation, charming puzzles, and clever meta elements make it an entertaining little spectacle that is well worth experiencing, even if only once. Rusty Lake manages to transform the simple idea of a magic show into a memorable interactive vignette that feels both playful and slightly mysterious.

[h3] A Quick Look at the Story [/h3]
In this anniversary entry, you’re invited to attend a magic show hosted by Mr. Rabbit. The game takes you through a series of performances that serve as a journey across the history of Rusty Lake. As you move from act to act, you revisit key moments and references from previous games while solving puzzles, collecting cards, and uncovering small secrets along the way.

[h3] In-Depth Review [/h3]
Celebrating the 10th anniversary of Rusty Lake felt like taking a step back into a surreal, familiar dream. This special game is more than just a collection of puzzles, it’s a love letter to longtime fans. The way it connects with the history of the series was very nostalgic. Revisiting moments, characters, and fragments from past titles made me feel like I was both playing something new and remembering all the good times I had exploring this universe before.

The puzzles are surprisingly intuitive compared to earlier entries from the studio. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing, it makes the experience flow more smoothly, allowing you to focus on the story and the atmosphere rather than getting stuck too often. The narrative itself is engaging, and the way the game encourages you to collect all the cards and achievements adds a nice extra layer of motivation to keep exploring.

One of the best parts is how the game lets you feel closer to the creators. There’s a certain charm and humor in the way everything is presented, and it manages to feel personal despite being part of a long-running series.

That said, not everything is perfect. Some of the show segments dragged on a bit longer than I would’ve liked. A smaller number of these would have made the pacing tighter and the experience even more enjoyable. While they added context and atmosphere, at times they felt like they were slowing down the momentum of the game.

Rusty lake/Cube Escape Review

After finally revisiting and catching up with this series from my last played game being Hotel I believe, I'm going to attempt to review the 18 entries as a whole. I feel it's the best way to look at the series. They are talked about roughly in the intended play order so read to where it's appropriate, some further thoughts on the whole series at the bottom.

Mr magic rabbit show was an okay fluff piece. At least it's free. I don't fund the puzzles very good (I'd struggle to call some of them puzzles, which makes it feel like a poor celebration of Rusty lake)

And that's kind of why I felt like I had to Tackle the game like this, you aren't just buying into one game but an over arching narrative that sadly in 13 years and 18 games we've seen so little forward momentum in, it feels like Roots was the last to really give any. They do easily could provide some answers close the odd mystery while keeping the rest alive but not only are we reiterating the same mystery the same point in the story but tacking on another mystery to the same thing. I'd be like if kingdom hearts one never had us save kairi and face ansem. Sure there was plenty more mystery but it was a self contained story that brought itself to a close.

So do I recommend it. Yes? Probably, there's some really great bits and even as a whole it adds up to a pretty okay price. The puzzles feel like they getting increasingly obtuse though, I'm not a fan of all this multimedia cross socials nonsense, the games should contain their own answers. It's very fad like but also wasn't it a fad before rusty lake was even a thing and wasn't popular then.

But to sum up my thoughts I want to discuss the games plot so mega spoilers maybe. To me the game is not to be taken at face value anywhere, it's all just a vehicle for it's narrative  and a glimpse into a mind that doesn't cope with the reality they've been dealt. So paradoxically the game has told us exactly what it was about from game 1. Mental health (rusty lake mental health), depression (van Gogh Laura even dale), nostalgia (the wallpapers the furniture the phones it's all so nostalgic even if a time you may not have experienced) and letting go, of the past, of paradise (even though it was never good), of anger (Albert) of guilt (Dale for both Laura and his parents, he's clearly seeing his failure to provide justice for her as him harming her, even though there is no mystery she took her own life it was her own dark self). Robert couldn't let go of something he didn't own and "lost it all". The Vanderbooms don't want to let go of life so badly they ruin multiple generations of their family with their nonsense. So I am going to take a que from this series and let go, of it, the developers might not be ready to yet and are stuck in this holding pattern, slapping in fads that don't move things forward but after 13 years I'm ready to let go, frankly I struggle to see how Servant of the lake being based when it is, will provide any answers we hadn't already seen in past games. Thanks for the many years of fun, short puzzle games. Readers be aware of the length of time and possible investment into this series you are making when so many of the games just repeating a pattern. Dale invested case 23 10 years ago (2015). And we still don't know what happened. So many of the games feel like a teaser for the next game...but it's not even this story line in the next product, and when it does come it's just providing a slightly different view of information we already had.

A wonderful celebration of the Rusty Lake series and the folks behind it.

I must say this game took me on a surprise rollercoaster, transforming from another Rusty Lake title to a package of easter eggs and details nodding to previous titles, as well as other game the Dev team has worked on outside of this series.

I was taken by surprise when the game transformed beyond the magic show into your character helping to continue 'developing' the game, within a game. My favorite details were in the office where you could take a look at various artifacts from the Rusty Lake series, both mainly on the shelves and scattered around the room. My personal favorite is the in-game photos on the phone of the Dev team, it's a personal favorite of mine when you get to see the team behind something within a title. I also love the attention to detail when the player interacts with the phone being able to break the 4th wall.

Overall, the length of the puzzles and their difficulty were just right. Although I did find the knife puzzle a bit trivial, the rest of the puzzles were very intuitive and followed a similar pattern known if you have played any previous titles. The Dev team and their Rusty Lake series will always hold a special place in my gaming history as one of the first titles that captivated mean back on flash alongside the Henry Stickman series and a Small Favor series.

The Mr. Rabbit Magic Show is a short, charming, and slightly creepy puzzle adventure that feels like a mini–Rusty Lake celebration. The atmosphere is great, the art and music hit that classic eerie vibe, and the 20 small acts keep things fun without dragging on. It’s simple, but polished — and for a free game, it delivers exactly what it promises: a weird, magical break that fans will enjoy.

If you like Rusty Lake or quick puzzle games, this is definitely worth playing.
